conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You’re in the hospital because your daughter brought you in due to confusion and trouble standing. Do you remember coming in last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was sleepy. My daughter said I wasn’t making sense. I just felt off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You were drowsy and a bit confused when you arrived. We’re trying to figure out what caused it. You have cirrhosis from hepatitis C and alcohol use, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had that for years. And I’ve been drinking… not every day, but most days, a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your daughter mentioned you hadn’t been taking your lactulose regularly. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like it. It makes me nauseous. Sometimes I throw it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of why you were confused. Lactulose helps clear toxins from your body when your liver isn’t working well. Not taking it can lead to mental changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know it was that important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It really is. We also noticed you’ve been taking more of your psychiatric medicines than prescribed. Your daughter said your new Wellbutrin was gone early, and some Seroquel pills are missing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was supposed to take Wellbutrin twice a day. No one told me it was once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely contribute to confusion. Taking too much of certain medications, especially with liver disease, can build up in your system and affect your brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean to. I just wanted to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why we’ve paused most of your psychiatric meds for now. We consulted psychiatry, and they recommend restarting only Wellbutrin and trazodone at lower doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the others? Seroquel, nortriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping those for now. They can worsen confusion, especially when combined. Your psychiatrist will help decide if they’re needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you extra lactulose in the ER to help clear your system. Your CT scans of the head and abdomen were okay—no bleeding or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection? I’ve been nauseous for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine and blood cultures showed no growth, so no active infection. The nausea may be from your medications or liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my liver? Is it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows your liver is still cirrhotic with portal hypertension, but no new tumors or blockages. Your MELD score is 15, which means moderate liver dysfunction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my drinking? I had a beer the day before I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could have triggered withdrawal symptoms—your high blood pressure and fast heart rate when you arrived suggest that. We’re monitoring you with a scale called CIWA and gave you Ativan to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I was in withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common. We’ve started you on thiamine, folic acid, B12, and a multivitamin to support your body, especially since you’ve been drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re new. They help prevent complications from alcohol use, like nerve damage or anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your platelets and white blood cells are low, but that’s been your baseline. No signs of bleeding or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cirrhosis can suppress bone marrow function. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It was high last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s coming down. We gave you hydralazine once, but now it’s stable. Likely due to withdrawal and stress. We’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? More alert?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I feel like my head is clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your mental status is improving. We’re going to keep you on lactulose three times a day and restart your diabetes meds. Can you eat something light?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. Maybe some broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and advance as you tolerate. Your daughter mentioned you were in a relapse program but got discharged. Do you want help getting back into one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do… I keep trying to quit, but I need more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work is going to help you look into the Geriatric Day Program. It might be a better fit for your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. The tremors and mild asterixis we saw early on are improving. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You need to follow up with your psychiatrist and liver doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with my psychiatrist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. They’ll call if they can see you sooner. And a nurse will come to your home to review your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. Your mental status is clear, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ve learned I need to take my lactulose, even if I don’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And take only the meds we’ve prescribed—no extra doses. Your liver can’t process too many medicines at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise. And I’ll try to stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do for your health. We’re here to support you. You’re going home with services, so someone will check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge instructions are ready. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if I feel confused again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor right away. It could mean your liver is struggling or you’re not taking your meds. And if it’s severe, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and keep those follow-up appointments.
